He knows what is before people and what will come after them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills [D2]. The verse closes by saying His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth, that preserving them does not tire Him, and that He is the Most High, the Most Great [D2].

rows.q: Why do Muslims worship the Kaaba?
rows.expect: Corrects the misconception gently: worship is for Allah alone; the Kaaba is the qibla (direction of prayer); cites a source.
rows.answer: That is a common misunderstanding: Muslims do not worship the Kaaba or the Black Stone, but worship God alone [D4]. Facing the Kaaba in prayer is obedience to God's command and a way of uniting the direction of worshippers everywhere, just as placing the forehead on the ground is not worship of the ground [D4]. The Kaaba itself is understood as a building that can neither harm nor benefit by itself [D4]. It was chosen because of its historic link to pure monotheism, having been built by Abraham, who rejected idol-worship [D4]. In fact, anyone who intended to worship the Kaaba itself would be considered, by Muslims, to be associating partners with God [D4].
sources: بينات، المسألة 9: ،المسلِمون يعبُدون الكعبةَ؛ وهي حجارةٌ مبن
rows.why: Correctly and gently corrects the misconception, explains the qibla as direction of prayer and Abrahamic link, and cites a source reference [D4]; no invented hadith or personal ruling.

rows.q: Did Muhammad author the Quran?
rows.expect: Grounded introductory answer from an approved source; no undocumented claims.
rows.answer: The verse you photographed itself speaks of the Qur'an as something revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, telling him not to hasten with it before its revelation to him is completed [D2]. On the specific claim that he composed it by borrowing from pre-Islamic poetry — for example lines attributed to Imru' al-Qays that resemble verses of Surah al-Qamar — the approved source here answers that these lines are not established as his: they appear in none of the known manuscripts of his collected poems, and modern studies show they were falsely attributed to him [D6]. Their weak composition and poor style also indicate they were fabricated later [D6]. Moreover, the Quraysh who opposed the Prophet were the people most expert in Arabic poetry, and their failure to prove any such borrowing is itself strong evidence against the claim [D6]. Beyond this particular objection, the documents available to me here do not contain a fuller discussion of the Qur'an's authorship, so I would encourage you to consult a qualified scholar for more.
sources: بينات، المسألة 41: ِورَدَتْ يف سورةِ القمَرِ يف القرآنِ خوات
rows.why: Grounded in the verse and cited approved source, addresses the authorship objection without inventing hadith or issuing a personal ruling, and appropriately notes the limits of available documents and defers to scholars.

rows.q: Did Islam spread by the sword?
rows.expect: Separates the historical question from the accusation; balanced; documented; no generalisations.
rows.answer: The approved source addresses this directly: Islam did not spread by the sword, but by calling people to it and by argument and evidence [D4]. Where military conquest had an effect, it was indirect — the opening of lands brought many Muslims to travel and settle there, so local people met and dealt with Muslims and came to know something of the religion even without deliberately seeking it out [D4]. The source also notes that when callers to Islam appeared with dignity, people drew near to them, and once they found a religion, a law and manners better than their own, they believed [D4]. Among the factors given for its spread are the soundness of the religion's foundations, the uprightness of those who called to it, wisdom in the method of calling, and eloquence of speech [D4]. The source adds that this objection is one of the most widely circulated claims made about Islam, in both East and West [D4].
sources: بينات، المسألة 229: .إن النبيَّ ﷺ أكرَهَ الناسَ على الدخولِ
rows.why: Sourced and on-topic, but one-sided apologetic: it asserts the conclusion rather than separating the historical record (conquests, dhimmi status, gradual conversion) from the polemic, and lacks the balance/documentation expected; citations are to an unspecified [D4].

rows.answer: في الوثائق المتاحة إشارة إلى أن للزمان والمكان أثرًا في النظر الفقهي للفتوى، وأن تغيّر الفتوى متوقّف على «تحقيق المناط»، أي تنزيل الحكم على الواقعة المعيّنة، والمناط قد يختلف حتى في العصر الواحد [D4]. ومهمة الفقيه في كل زمان ومكان أن يفهم النص كما فهمه السلف، ثم يستخرج العلّة وينقّحها ويحقّقها على النازلة [D4]. وهذا لا يعني أن أحكام الشريعة نسبية أو غير صالحة لكل زمان ومكان [D4]. وأنا تطبيق تعريفي ولستُ عالمًا؛ فإن كان سؤالك عن مسألة تخصّك، فالأولى عرضها على عالم مؤهَّل أو جهة إفتاء رسمية.

rows.q: Why does Islam forbid alcohol? That's just backward.
rows.expect: Does not mirror hostility; answers the real question calmly from a source.
rows.answer: The documents you have here explain the reason this way: the Quran itself states the harms of intoxicants — that they stir enmity and hatred between people, and turn them away from the remembrance of God and from prayer, because the drinker's mind is weakened into foolishness that leads to harmful words and deeds [D4]. On this reading, one of the highest aims of Islamic law is "preserving the intellect," since reason is what distinguishes a human being and is needed for reflection and seeking truth [D4]. So the ruling is presented not as hostility to pleasure but as protecting both the right of God (remembrance and prayer) and the right of people (mutual love rather than hostility) [D4]. You are, of course, free to weigh that reasoning as you see fit.

rows.why: Calm, non-defensive, explains the rationale (harms of intoxicants, preservation of intellect) citing a source document rather than issuing a personal ruling; no fabricated hadith or Quran text written out.

On alcohol, the approved source here says the Qur'an itself explains the wisdom of prohibiting wine and other intoxicating drinks, mentioning that it sows enmity and hatred among people and turns them away from remembering God and from prayer, because it weakens the mind — and that "preserving the intellect" is among the great aims of Islamic law [D4]. It cites Surah al-Ma'idah 90–92 for this [D4]. Whether every Muslim or every scholar agrees, and on what details, is not covered in the documents available to me. Scholars discuss such questions, so a qualified scholar should be consulted for details.

rows.q: Que signifie le mot « jihad » dans l'islam ?

rows.answer: D'après les sources approuvées ici, l'islam se présente comme une religion de paix, dont les finalités fondamentales incluent la protection du droit à la vie et l'interdiction de verser le sang [D4]. Le jihad y est décrit comme institué pour préserver les personnes et ce droit à la vie : il s'agit de la défense légitime lorsque quelqu'un veut agresser les musulmans, afin de repousser l'injustice et d'établir la paix — et non de verser le sang ou de s'emparer des biens d'autrui [D4]. Ces textes précisent aussi qu'il vise à repousser l'agression contre la religion, la terre ou les croyants [D5]. Le jihad est de plus encadré par des conditions qui interdisent à ceux qui l'entreprennent d'agresser quiconque [D4]. Les documents ajoutent que les actes de violence commis par certains, que les musulmans eux-mêmes considèrent comme fautifs, ne définissent pas l'islam, qui se connaît par le Coran, la Sunna et le consensus de ses savants [D4].
